decks.title: Compound, Multiple and Sub-multiple Angles - Part 1: Addition formulae and multiple angles
goals: Expand the sine, cosine, tangent and cotangent of a sum or difference of two angles
Find exact values such as sine 75 degrees and tangent 15 degrees
Use the formula for tangent of A plus B plus C
Write the double and triple angle formulae and use them in values and proofs

slides.heading: Compound, Multiple and Sub-multiple Angles, Part 1
slides.body_md: From the angles you know to the angles you can build.

nodes.label: Why sums of angles need formulae

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: why sums of angles need formulae, sine and cosine of A plus or minus B, tangent and cotangent and the three-angle sum, the double angle, and the triple angle.
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance.

slides.narration: Welcome to part one. You know the sine and cosine of thirty, forty five and sixty degrees. In this part you learn how to find the values for sums and differences of these angles, and then for double and triple angles, using one family of formulae.

slides.heading: Why a sum of angles needs a formula
slides.body_md: It is tempting to write $\sin(A + B) = \sin A + \sin B$. The table shows that this fails for every pair we try, so we need the true formula.

visual.alt: Table of four angle pairs showing that the sine of a sum is not the sum of the sines: for 30 and 60 degrees the left side is 1.0000 and the right side is 1.3660, and the other pairs also differ.
visual.caption: Sine does not distribute over a sum.

slides.narration: Try the idea that the sine of a sum is the sum of the sines. At thirty and sixty degrees the left side is exactly one but the right side is more than one point three. Other pairs also disagree. The sine function does not split over addition, and the next slides give the correct rule.

slides.heading: The unit circle gives cos(A minus B)
slides.body_md: Points $P$ and $Q$ at angles $A$ and $B$, and $R$ at angle $A - B$, are on the unit circle. Chord $PQ$ and chord $XR$ subtend the same angle at $O$.
bullets: $PQ^2 = (\cos A - \cos B)^2 + (\sin A - \sin B)^2 = 2 - 2(\cos A\cos B + \sin A\sin B)$
Equal chords give $\cos(A - B) = \cos A\cos B + \sin A\sin B$

visual.alt: Unit circle with the points P at angle A, Q at angle B and R at angle A minus B measured from the positive x-axis. The chord PQ and the chord from the point (1, 0) to R are drawn; they subtend equal angles at the centre, so they have equal length.
visual.caption: Chord $PQ$ = chord from $(1, 0)$ to $R$: this gives $\cos(A - B)$.

slides.narration: Place the points on the unit circle. The chord from P to Q and the chord from the point one, zero to R both span the same angle at the centre, so they are equal. Write each squared length with coordinates, simplify using sine squared plus cosine squared equals one, and compare. The result is the cosine of A minus B.

slides.heading: Sine and cosine of a sum and a difference
slides.body_md: Replace $B$ by $-B$ in the cosine result, and use $\sin\theta = \cos(90^\circ - \theta)$, to obtain the four formulae.

visual.alt: Table of the four sine and cosine addition formulae with a numerical check at A equal 75 degrees and B equal 40 degrees: for instance sine of 115 degrees is 0.9063 and equals sine 75 cosine 40 plus cosine 75 sine 40.
visual.caption: Cosine changes the sign between the two products; sine keeps it.

slides.narration: From the cosine of A minus B we get the other three. Replacing B by minus B gives the cosine of A plus B. Writing sine as cosine of ninety degrees minus the angle gives the sine formulae. The table checks all four at seventy five and forty degrees, and each pair of values agrees to four decimal places.

slides.heading: Quick check: a false rule
slides.body_md: Decide whether the sine of a sum can equal the sum of the sines for all angles.
slides.narration: Recall the table of four angle pairs and decide whether one counter example is enough.

slides.heading: Tangent and cotangent of A plus B and A minus B
slides.body_md: Divide $\sin(A \pm B)$ by $\cos(A \pm B)$ and divide top and bottom by $\cos A\cos B$ to get the tangent formulae; the cotangent formulae come from dividing by $\sin A\sin B$.

rows: $A,\ B,\ A + B \ne (2n + 1)\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and $\tan A\tan B \ne 1$
$A,\ B,\ A - B \ne (2n + 1)\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and $\tan A\tan B \ne -1$
$A,\ B,\ A + B \ne n\pi$ and $\cot A + \cot B \ne 0$
$A,\ B,\ A - B \ne n\pi$ and $\cot B \ne \cot A$

visual.alt: Table of the tangent and cotangent addition and subtraction formulae with their validity conditions: the angles and their sum or difference must lie where the function is defined, and the denominator must not be zero.
visual.caption: Each quotient formula needs its denominator to be non-zero.

slides.narration: Divide the sine formula by the cosine formula, then divide every term by cosine A times cosine B. The tangent formulae appear. For cotangent divide by sine A times sine B instead. Each formula holds only where the functions are defined and the denominator is not zero, so check that before using it.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: exact values
slides.body_md: Find the exact values of $\sin 75^\circ$ and $\tan 15^\circ$.

visual.alt: Worked example 1 table: sine of 75 degrees from 45 plus 30 degrees equals root 6 plus root 2 over 4, and tangent of 15 degrees from 60 minus 45 degrees equals 2 minus root 3.
visual.caption: Choose a split into angles whose values you know.

slides.narration: Split seventy five degrees as forty five plus thirty, and use the sine of a sum with the known values. For the tangent of fifteen degrees, split as sixty minus forty five. The quotient root three minus one over root three plus one becomes two minus root three after rationalising the denominator.

slides.heading: Quick check: a collapsing sum
slides.body_md: Recognise an addition formula in reverse.
slides.narration: Read the expression from right to left as the sine of a sum.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: from given ratios
slides.body_md: $\sin A = \dfrac{12}{37}$ with $A$ acute and $\cos B = -\dfrac{16}{65}$ with $B$ in quadrant II. Find $\sin(A + B)$ and $\cos(A + B)$ and the quadrant of $A + B$.
bullets: $\cos(A + B) = -\dfrac{1316}{2405}$: sine positive, cosine negative, so quadrant II

visual.alt: Worked example 2 table: sine A is 12 over 37 with A acute, cosine B is minus 16 over 65 with B in the second quadrant. Then cosine A is 35 over 37, sine B is 63 over 65, sine of A plus B is 2013 over 2405 and cosine of A plus B is minus 1316 over 2405, so A plus B is in the second quadrant.
visual.caption: Sine positive and cosine negative: $A + B$ lies in quadrant II.

slides.narration: First find the missing ratios, taking the sign from the quadrant. Cosine of A is thirty five over thirty seven. Sine of B is positive, sixty three over sixty five. Then substitute into the two formulae. The sine of the sum is positive and the cosine is negative, so the sum lies in the second quadrant.

slides.heading: Tangent of A plus B plus C
slides.body_md: Write $A + B + C = (A + B) + C$ and apply the tangent formula twice. When $A + B + C = 180^\circ$, the numerator must vanish because $\tan 180^\circ = 0$.

rows: $\tan(A + B + C) = \dfrac{\tan A + \tan B + \tan C - \tan A\tan B\tan C}{1 - \tan A\tan B - \tan B\tan C - \tan C\tan A}$
defined when the denominator is not zero
$\tan A + \tan B + \tan C = \tan A\tan B\tan C$

visual.alt: Table for the sum of three angles: the general formula for tangent of A plus B plus C, and the special case A plus B plus C equal to 180 degrees where the sum of the tangents equals their product; for 40, 65 and 75 degrees both are 6.7157.
visual.caption: The special case follows because $\tan 180^\circ = 0$.

slides.narration: Treat A plus B as one angle and add C. The result has the three tangents in the numerator, minus the product of all three, over one minus the sum of the pairwise products. When the three angles add up to one hundred eighty degrees the tangent is zero, so the sum of the tangents equals their product.

slides.heading: Quick check: angles of a triangle
slides.body_md: Use the three-angle result for the angles of a triangle.
slides.narration: The three angles of a triangle add up to one hundred eighty degrees.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: proving an identity
slides.body_md: Prove that $\dfrac{\sin(A + B)}{\cos A\cos B} = \tan A + \tan B$.
bullets: Expand the numerator by the addition formula
Split into two fractions and cancel

rows: $\dfrac{\sin A\cos B + \cos A\sin B}{\cos A\cos B}$
$\dfrac{\sin A\cos B}{\cos A\cos B} + \dfrac{\cos A\sin B}{\cos A\cos B}$
$\dfrac{\sin A}{\cos A} + \dfrac{\sin B}{\cos B} = \tan A + \tan B$

visual.alt: Worked example 3 table proving that sine of A plus B over cosine A cosine B equals tangent A plus tangent B: expand the numerator, split the fraction, cancel; at A equal 35 degrees and B equal 20 degrees both sides equal 1.0642.
visual.caption: Left side to right side in three moves.

slides.narration: Start from the left side. Expand sine of A plus B in the numerator. Split into two fractions: in each, one trigonometric factor cancels with the denominator, leaving tangent A and tangent B. A numerical check at thirty five and twenty degrees gives the same number on both sides.

slides.heading: Double angle formulae
slides.body_md: Put $B = A$ in the sum formulae. The cosine has three forms; choose the one that uses what you are given.

rows: $\cos^2 x - \sin^2 x = 2\cos^2 x - 1 = 1 - 2\sin^2 x = \dfrac{1 - \tan^2 x}{1 + \tan^2 x}$

visual.alt: Table of the double angle formulae, each obtained by putting B equal to A in the addition formulae: sine 2x, the four forms of cosine 2x, and tangent 2x.
visual.caption: Choose the cosine form that uses what is given.

slides.narration: Setting B equal to A turns each addition formula into a double angle formula. Sine of two x is two sine x cosine x. Cosine of two x has three forms, using cosine squared minus sine squared, or only cosine, or only sine. Tangent of two x is two tangent x over one minus tangent squared x.

slides.heading: sin 2x and 2 sin x cos x are one curve
slides.body_md: The graph of $y = \sin 2x$ has period $\pi$, twice as fast as $\sin x$, and the product $2\sin x\cos x$ traces exactly the same curve.

visual.alt: The graphs of y equal sine 2x and y equal 2 sine x cosine x from 0 to 6.6. They are one and the same curve: two full waves between 0 and 2 pi, with peaks of height 1 at pi over 4 and 5 pi over 4 and troughs of depth minus 1 at 3 pi over 4 and 7 pi over 4.
visual.caption: The two expressions draw the same wave of period $\pi$.

slides.narration: Here are the graphs of sine two x and of two sine x cosine x on the same axes. They lie on top of each other, which is what an identity means graphically. The wave has period pi, so it completes two cycles between zero and two pi, with peaks and troughs of height one.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: double angle from cos x
slides.body_md: If $\cos x = -\dfrac{7}{25}$ and $x$ is in quadrant III, find $\sin 2x$, $\cos 2x$ and $\tan 2x$.

rows: third quadrant: sine negative, from $\sin^2 x = 1 - \dfrac{49}{625}$

visual.alt: Worked example 4 table: cosine x is minus 7 over 25 with x in the third quadrant. Then sine x is minus 24 over 25, sine 2x is 336 over 625, cosine 2x is minus 527 over 625 and tangent 2x is minus 336 over 527.
visual.caption: The sign of $\sin x$ comes from the quadrant of $x$.

slides.narration: Find sine x first. In the third quadrant it is negative, minus twenty four over twenty five. Then apply the double angle formulae. Sine of two x is a product of two negatives, so it is positive. Cosine of two x is negative. The tangent is their quotient, minus three hundred thirty six over five hundred twenty seven.

slides.heading: Quick check: a double angle value
slides.body_md: Find the cosine of a double angle from the cosine of the angle.
slides.narration: Choose the form of cosine two x that uses only cosine.

slides.heading: Triple angle formulae
slides.body_md: Write $3x = 2x + x$. Each formula is a cubic in the same function of $x$.

visual.alt: Table of the triple angle formulae: sine 3x is 3 sine x minus 4 sine cubed x, cosine 3x is 4 cosine cubed x minus 3 cosine x, and tangent 3x is 3 tangent x minus tangent cubed x over 1 minus 3 tangent squared x; each comes from writing 3x as 2x plus x.
visual.caption: Write $3x = 2x + x$ and use the double angle formulae.

slides.narration: Write three x as two x plus x and expand. For sine, replace cosine squared by one minus sine squared and you get three sine x minus four sine cubed x. For cosine, do the same with sine squared and you get four cosine cubed x minus three cosine x. The tangent formula comes from the tangent addition rule.

slides.heading: cos 3x as a cubic in cos x
slides.body_md: The curve $y = \cos 3x$ makes three waves in $2\pi$, and the cubic $4\cos^3 x - 3\cos x$ draws it too.

visual.alt: The graphs of y equal cosine 3x and y equal 4 cosine cubed x minus 3 cosine x from 0 to 6.5. They coincide: three full waves between 0 and 2 pi, with value 1 at 0, 2 pi over 3 and 4 pi over 3 and value minus 1 at pi over 3, pi and 5 pi over 3.
visual.caption: Three waves in $2\pi$: the cubic in $\cos x$ draws the same curve.

slides.narration: The graph shows cosine three x and the cubic expression in cosine x. They coincide. Three waves fit in a full turn, so the peaks at zero, two pi over three and four pi over three have height one, and the troughs between them have depth minus one. The cubic form is the key to the one third angle formulae later.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: a triple angle identity
slides.body_md: Prove that $\cos 3A = \cos A\,(2\cos 2A - 1)$.
bullets: Factor $\cos A$ out of $4\cos^3 A - 3\cos A$

rows: Start from the triple angle formula

visual.alt: Worked example 5 table proving that cosine 3A equals cosine A times the bracket 2 cosine 2A minus 1: factor cosine A from the triple angle formula, rewrite the bracket with the double angle formula, and check at A equal 25 degrees where both sides are 0.2588.
visual.caption: The check at $25^\circ$ agrees to four places.

slides.narration: Start from cosine three A written in cosine only, and factor out cosine A. The bracket is four cosine squared A minus three. Write it as two times the bracket two cosine squared A minus one, minus one. The inner bracket is cosine two A, so the bracket equals two cosine two A minus one.

slides.heading: Quick check: a triple angle value
slides.body_md: Evaluate the triple angle formula at a special angle.
slides.narration: Substitute thirty degrees into the sine formula and compare with sine of ninety degrees.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: $\sin(A \pm B)$, $\cos(A \mp B)$ keep the sign as shown
$A + B + C = 180^\circ$: $\tan A + \tan B + \tan C = \tan A\tan B\tan C$

visual.alt: Summary flow of Part 1: the addition formulae, the double angle formulae from B equal to A, the triple angle formulae from 2x plus x, and a numerical check at a chosen angle.
visual.caption: Part 1 in one line.

slides.narration: To sum up. The addition formulae give sine, cosine, tangent and cotangent of sums and differences. Putting the two angles equal gives the double angle formulae, and writing three x as two x plus x gives the triple angle formulae. Always check the formula with a numerical angle before relying on it.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Find the missing ratio with the **correct sign** from the quadrant
The cosine formula changes the sign between the two products
Check a tangent formula for **zero denominators**
Test any identity you prove at one numerical angle

headers: How ISC marks are usually given
rows: split of the angle 1, correct surd 1

visual.alt: Exam tips table for Part 1: exact values earn the split and the surd, given-ratio questions earn the missing ratios, the formula and the answer, identities earn the expansion, simplification and conclusion, and multiple angle values earn the formula, substitution and answer.
visual.caption: Always find the missing ratio with the correct sign.

slides.narration: In the examination, find the missing ratio with the correct sign, using the quadrant. Remember that the cosine addition formula changes the sign between its two products. Look out for zero denominators in tangent formulae. And once you have proved an identity, test it at one numerical angle to catch slips.

decks.title: Compound, Multiple and Sub-multiple Angles - Part 2: Half-angle, one-third angle and product formulae
goals: Use the half-angle formulae and decide the sign from the quadrant
Use the one-third angle relations to form and solve cubics
Change a sum or difference of sines or cosines into a product
Change a product of sines or cosines into a sum or difference

slides.heading: Compound, Multiple and Sub-multiple Angles, Part 2
slides.body_md: Halves, thirds, and the exchange between sums and products.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: half-angle formulae, one-third angle formulae, sums of sines and cosines turned into products, and products turned into sums.
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. You will find the trigonometric ratios of half an angle and one third of an angle, and learn to exchange sums and products of sines and cosines. These tools finish most proofs and exact value questions in this chapter.

slides.heading: Half-angle formulae
slides.body_md: Use $\cos 2\theta = 1 - 2\sin^2\theta = 2\cos^2\theta - 1$ with $\theta = \dfrac{x}{2}$. The formulae give **squares**.

visual.alt: Table of the half-angle formulae with a numerical check at x equal 100 degrees: sine squared of 50 degrees is 0.5868, cosine squared is 0.4132, tangent squared is 1.4203 and tangent is 1.1918, each on both sides.
visual.caption: Half-angle values come as squares, so the sign needs a separate decision.

slides.narration: Take the double angle formulae for cosine and put theta equal to x over two. Solving for sine squared and cosine squared gives the first two lines. Dividing them gives the tangent squared formula, and the last line expresses tangent of half an angle without a square root. The table checks each at one hundred degrees.

slides.heading: The sign of a half-angle
slides.body_md: A formula for $\sin^2\dfrac{x}{2}$ gives only the size. The sign depends on the **quadrant of $\dfrac{x}{2}$**, not of $x$.

visual.alt: Table of the signs of the half-angle ratios for x between 0 and 360 degrees: half of x lies in the first quadrant when x is below 180 degrees, where all three ratios are positive, and in the second quadrant when x is between 180 and 360 degrees, where sine is positive and cosine and tangent are negative.
visual.caption: Decide the quadrant of $\dfrac{x}{2}$ first, then the sign.

slides.narration: If x lies between zero and ninety, or ninety and one hundred eighty degrees, half of x is in the first quadrant and all three ratios are positive. If x lies between one hundred eighty and three hundred sixty degrees, half of x is in the second quadrant, so the sine is positive but cosine and tangent are negative.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: the angle 22.5 degrees
slides.body_md: Find $\sin 22.5^\circ$, $\cos 22.5^\circ$ and $\tan 22.5^\circ$ exactly.
bullets: $22.5^\circ = \dfrac{45^\circ}{2}$, an acute angle, so every root is positive

visual.alt: Worked example 1 table: using x equal 45 degrees in the half-angle formulae, cosine 22.5 degrees is root of 2 plus root 2 over 2, sine 22.5 degrees is root of 2 minus root 2 over 2, and tangent 22.5 degrees is root 2 minus 1; the angle is acute, so every root is positive.
visual.caption: An acute angle takes the positive root.

slides.narration: Take x equal to forty five degrees. The cosine squared of the half angle is one plus root two over two, all over two, which is two plus root two over four. Take the positive root, since twenty two point five degrees is acute. The tangent avoids a nested root and simplifies to root two minus one.

slides.heading: Quick check: the half-angle square
slides.body_md: Evaluate a half-angle square from a given cosine.
slides.narration: Use the formula for cosine squared of half an angle.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: half-angle values from cos x
slides.body_md: If $\cos x = \dfrac{7}{25}$ and $270^\circ < x < 360^\circ$, find $\sin\dfrac{x}{2}$, $\cos\dfrac{x}{2}$ and $\tan\dfrac{x}{2}$.
bullets: $\dfrac{x}{2}$ is in quadrant II: sine positive, cosine negative

visual.alt: Worked example 2 table: cosine x is 7 over 25 with x between 270 and 360 degrees, so x over 2 is in the second quadrant; sine of x over 2 is 3 over 5, cosine of x over 2 is minus 4 over 5 and tangent of x over 2 is minus 3 over 4.
visual.caption: Quadrant first: in quadrant II cosine and tangent are negative.

slides.narration: Decide the quadrant first. Half of an angle between two hundred seventy and three hundred sixty degrees lies between one hundred thirty five and one hundred eighty, in the second quadrant. Sine squared is nine over twenty five, so sine is three fifths. Cosine squared is sixteen over twenty five, so cosine is minus four fifths.

slides.heading: One-third angle formulae
slides.body_md: The triple angle formulae with $y = \dfrac{x}{3}$ give $\sin x$, $\cos x$ and $\tan x$ in terms of $\sin y$, $\cos y$, $\tan y$. Read backwards, each is a **cubic** for the one-third angle.

visual.alt: Table of the one-third angle relations: the triple angle formulae read with y equal x over 3, which turn sine x, cosine x and tangent x into cubics satisfied by sine, cosine and tangent of x over 3.
visual.caption: The triple angle formula, read backwards, is a cubic for $x/3$.

slides.narration: There is no simple square root formula for a third of an angle. Instead, we use the triple angle formula backwards. If x is known, the sine of x over three satisfies a cubic equation, and the three roots correspond to three different angles whose triples have the same sine.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a cubic from cos 3 theta
slides.body_md: Show that $\cos 20^\circ$, $\cos 140^\circ$ and $\cos 260^\circ$ are roots of $8c^3 - 6c - 1 = 0$.

visual.alt: Worked example 3 table: for 20, 140 and 260 degrees the angle 3 theta is 60, 420 and 780 degrees, all with cosine one half, so cosine theta is a root of 8c cubed minus 6c minus 1; the values 0.9397, minus 0.1736 and minus 0.7660 each give 0 in the cubic.
visual.caption: Three angles, one cubic: the roots sum to $0$ and multiply to $\dfrac{1}{8}$.

slides.narration: For each of the three angles, three times the angle differs from sixty degrees by a whole number of turns, so the cosine of the triple angle is one half. Put that into the triple angle formula and multiply by two. All three cosines satisfy the same cubic, and the table confirms each value.

slides.heading: The three roots on the graph
slides.body_md: The cubic $y = 8x^3 - 6x - 1$ meets the $x$-axis exactly three times, at the cosines of the three angles.

visual.alt: Graph of y equal 8 x cubed minus 6 x minus 1 for x from minus 1.2 to 1.2. The curve crosses the x-axis three times, at about minus 0.766, minus 0.174 and 0.940, which are the cosines of 140, 260 and 20 degrees.
visual.caption: The three roots are $\cos 20^\circ$, $\cos 140^\circ$ and $\cos 260^\circ$.

slides.narration: The graph of the cubic crosses the horizontal axis three times, at about minus zero point seven seven, minus zero point one seven and zero point nine four. These are the cosines of one hundred forty, two hundred sixty and twenty degrees. A cubic has at most three roots, so there are no other values.

slides.heading: Quick check: roots of the cubic
slides.body_md: Apply the sum of the roots of this cubic.
slides.narration: The sum of the roots of a cubic comes from the coefficient of x squared, which is zero here.

slides.heading: Sum and difference to product
slides.body_md: Put $A + B = C$ and $A - B = D$ in the product formulae, so that $A = \dfrac{C + D}{2}$ and $B = \dfrac{C - D}{2}$.

visual.alt: Table of the four sum and difference to product formulae with a check at C equal 110 degrees and D equal 30 degrees: for example sine 110 plus sine 30 is 1.4397 on both sides, and cosine 110 minus cosine 30 is minus 1.2080 on both sides.
visual.caption: Only $\cos C - \cos D$ has a minus sign in front.

slides.narration: To turn a sum of two sines or cosines into a product, use the half sum and half difference of the two angles. The sum of sines becomes two sine of half sum times cosine of half difference. For the difference of cosines there is a minus sign, and the two sines appear.

slides.heading: The product form shows the envelope
slides.body_md: $\sin 5x + \sin 3x = 2\sin 4x\cos x$: a fast wave $\sin 4x$ inside the slow envelope $\pm 2\cos x$.

visual.alt: The graph of y equal sine 5x plus sine 3x from 0 to 6.4 with the curves y equal 2 cosine x and y equal minus 2 cosine x. The fast wave sine 4x is enclosed by these two slow curves, because the sum equals 2 sine 4x cosine x.
visual.caption: The product form shows the slow envelope $\pm 2\cos x$ and the fast wave $\sin 4x$.

slides.narration: Here is the graph of sine five x plus sine three x. It looks complicated as a sum, but as a product it is two cosine x times sine four x. The slow curve two cosine x and its mirror image enclose the fast wave, which is how beats arise when two notes of nearby pitch sound together.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a quotient of sums
slides.body_md: Prove that $\dfrac{\sin 7x + \sin 3x}{\cos 7x + \cos 3x} = \tan 5x$.
bullets: Half sum $= 5x$, half difference $= 2x$ in both

visual.alt: Worked example 4 table proving that sine 7x plus sine 3x over cosine 7x plus cosine 3x equals tangent 5x: turn the numerator and the denominator into products, cancel 2 cosine 2x, and check at x equal 8 degrees where both sides are 0.8391.
visual.caption: Pair the angles so that the half-sum is the same in both.

slides.narration: Use the same pair in the numerator and the denominator. The half sum of seven x and three x is five x, and the half difference is two x. The numerator becomes two sine five x cosine two x, and the denominator becomes two cosine five x cosine two x. Cancel the common factors and the tangent of five x remains.

slides.heading: Quick check: a sum as a product
slides.body_md: Complete a sum-to-product formula.
slides.narration: Find the half sum of the two angles.

slides.heading: Product to sum and difference
slides.body_md: Add and subtract the addition formulae: for example $\sin(A + B) + \sin(A - B) = 2\sin A\cos B$.

visual.alt: Table of the four product to sum formulae with a check at A equal 65 degrees and B equal 20 degrees: for example 2 sine 65 cosine 20 is 1.7033 and equals sine 85 plus sine 45, also 1.7033.
visual.caption: Add or subtract the two addition formulae to get these.

slides.narration: The product formulae are the addition formulae read backwards. Adding the sine of A plus B and the sine of A minus B leaves two sine A cosine B. Subtracting leaves two cosine A sine B. For cosines, adding gives two cosine A cosine B, and subtracting gives two sine A sine B, with the order of the terms as in the table.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: exact products
slides.body_md: Find the exact values of $\cos 75^\circ\cos 15^\circ$, $\sin 105^\circ\cos 45^\circ$ and $\sin 135^\circ\sin 15^\circ$.
bullets: Write each product as half of a sum or difference of values at **standard angles**
No factor needs its own value

visual.alt: Worked example 5 table: cosine 75 cosine 15 equals one quarter, sine 105 cosine 45 equals 1 plus root 3 over 4, and sine 135 sine 15 equals root 3 minus 1 over 4, each found by turning the product into a sum of values at 90, 150, 60, 120 and 150 degrees.
visual.caption: Each product is evaluated without using the value of either factor.

slides.narration: For the first, the sum of the angles is ninety and the difference is sixty, so the product is half of cosine ninety plus cosine sixty, which is one quarter. For the second, the angles one hundred fifty and sixty give one plus root three over four. For the third, use the cosine difference form with one hundred twenty and one hundred fifty.

slides.heading: A difference of cosines as a product
slides.body_md: $\cos x - \cos 5x = 2\sin 3x\sin 2x$: the wave changes sign each time $\sin 2x$ does.

visual.alt: The graphs of y equal cosine x minus cosine 5x and y equal 2 sine 3x sine 2x from 0 to 6.4. The two curves lie on top of each other, a wave of height up to 2 that changes sign as sine 2x does.
visual.caption: Sum or product: one curve, two descriptions.

slides.narration: Both expressions are drawn here and they give the same curve. The difference of the cosines is simply a product of two sines. The curve is zero wherever either factor is zero, so the zeros are easiest to read from the product form.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: an identity with A

sections.heading: 1. Why we need addition formulae
sections.body_md:
The trigonometric ratios do **not** split over addition: $\sin(A + B) \ne \sin A + \sin B$ in general. For example $\sin 90^\circ = 1$ but $\sin 30^\circ + \sin 60^\circ \approx 1.366$.

The key result is $\cos(A - B) = \cos A\cos B + \sin A\sin B$, proved on the unit circle by equating the chords $PQ$ and $XR$. Everything else in this chapter follows from it by substitution.

key_terms.definition_md: An angle written as a sum or difference of two angles, such as $A + B$ or $A - B$.
An angle such as $2x$ or $3x$, a whole-number multiple of $x$.

visual.alt: Table of four angle pairs showing that the sine of a sum is not the sum of the sines: for 30 and 60 degrees the left side is 1.0000 and the right side is 1.3660, and the other pairs also differ.
visual.caption: Sine does not distribute over a sum.

visuals.caption: Chord $PQ$ = chord from $(1, 0)$ to $R$: this gives $\cos(A - B)$.

sections.heading: 2. Sine and cosine of A plus or minus B
sections.body_md:
Replace $B$ by $-B$ to get $\cos(A + B)$; use $\sin\theta = \cos(90^\circ - \theta)$ to get the sine formulae.

Sine formulae keep the sign of the angle ($\sin(A + B)$ has a plus between its products); cosine formulae reverse it. They give exact values at angles such as $15^\circ$, $75^\circ$, $105^\circ$, once you split the angle into two angles with known ratios.

key_terms.definition_md: Sine: same sign as the angle; cosine: opposite sign.

visual.alt: Table of the four sine and cosine addition formulae with a numerical check at A equal 75 degrees and B equal 40 degrees: for instance sine of 115 degrees is 0.9063 and equals sine 75 cosine 40 plus cosine 75 sine 40.
visual.caption: Cosine changes the sign between the two products; sine keeps it.

sections.heading: 3. Tangent, cotangent and tan(A + B + C)
sections.body_md:
Divide sine by cosine, then top and bottom by $\cos A\cos B$, to get the tangent formulae; divide by $\sin A\sin B$ for cotangent. Each holds only where the functions are defined and the denominator is not zero.

For three angles, $\tan(A + B + C) = \dfrac{\tan A + \tan B + \tan C - \tan A\tan B\tan C}{1 - \tan A\tan B - \tan B\tan C - \tan C\tan A}$. If $A + B + C = 180^\circ$ (angles of a triangle), then $\tan A + \tan B + \tan C = \tan A\tan B\tan C$.

key_terms.definition_md: The angles and the sum or difference must not be odd multiples of $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ (tangent) or multiples of $\pi$ (cotangent).

sections.heading: 4. Double angle formulae
sections.body_md:
Putting $B = A$ gives $\sin 2x = 2\sin x\cos x$ and $\cos 2x = \cos^2 x - \sin^2 x$, which has two further forms, $2\cos^2 x - 1$ and $1 - 2\sin^2 x$, and $\tan 2x = \dfrac{2\tan x}{1 - \tan^2 x}$. In terms of $t = \tan x$: $\sin 2x = \dfrac{2t}{1 + t^2}$ and $\cos 2x = \dfrac{1 - t^2}{1 + t^2}$.

The sign of $\sin x$ or $\cos x$ is decided by the quadrant of $x$ before you substitute.

key_terms.definition_md: The angle $2x$; its ratios follow from the addition formulae with $B = A$.

rows: $\cos^2 x - \sin^2 x = 2\cos^2 x - 1 = 1 - 2\sin^2 x = \dfrac{1 - \tan^2 x}{1 + \tan^2 x}$

sections.heading: 5. Triple angle formulae
sections.body_md:
Write $3x = 2x + x$ and use the double angle formulae: $\sin 3x = 3\sin x - 4\sin^3 x$, $\cos 3x = 4\cos^3 x - 3\cos x$, $\tan 3x = \dfrac{3\tan x - \tan^3 x}{1 - 3\tan^2 x}$.

Useful rewritings: $\dfrac{\sin 3x}{\sin x} = 3 - 4\sin^2 x$ and $\cos 3x = \cos x\,(2\cos 2x - 1)$.

key_terms.definition_md: The angle $3x$; its sine and cosine are cubic expressions in $\sin x$ and $\cos x$.

visual.alt: Table of the triple angle formulae: sine 3x is 3 sine x minus 4 sine cubed x, cosine 3x is 4 cosine cubed x minus 3 cosine x, and tangent 3x is 3 tangent x minus tangent cubed x over 1 minus 3 tangent squared x; each comes from writing 3x as 2x plus x.

sections.heading: 6. Half-angle and one-third angle formulae
sections.body_md:
From $\cos x = 1 - 2\sin^2\dfrac{x}{2} = 2\cos^2\dfrac{x}{2} - 1$: $\sin^2\dfrac{x}{2} = \dfrac{1 - \cos x}{2}$, $\cos^2\dfrac{x}{2} = \dfrac{1 + \cos x}{2}$, $\tan\dfrac{x}{2} = \dfrac{1 - \cos x}{\sin x} = \dfrac{\sin x}{1 + \cos x}$. The **sign** of a root is that of the ratio in the quadrant of $\dfrac{x}{2}$.

With $y = \dfrac{x}{3}$, the triple angle formulae say $\sin x = 3\sin y - 4\sin^3 y$ and $\cos x = 4\cos^3 y - 3\cos y$; read backwards, the sine, cosine or tangent of $\dfrac{x}{3}$ is a root of a cubic whose other roots belong to the angles $\dfrac{x + 360^\circ k}{3}$.

key_terms.definition_md: Gives the square of a ratio of $\dfrac{x}{2}$; the quadrant of $\dfrac{x}{2}$ fixes the sign.

visual.caption: Half-angle values come as squares, so the sign needs a separate decision.

sections.heading: 7. Sum to product and product to sum
sections.body_md:
Put $C = A + B$, $D = A - B$ in the product formulae: $\sin C + \sin D = 2\sin\dfrac{C + D}{2}\cos\dfrac{C - D}{2}$, $\sin C - \sin D = 2\cos\dfrac{C + D}{2}\sin\dfrac{C - D}{2}$, $\cos C + \cos D = 2\cos\dfrac{C + D}{2}\cos\dfrac{C - D}{2}$, $\cos C - \cos D = -2\sin\dfrac{C + D}{2}\sin\dfrac{C - D}{2}$.

Read the other way: $2\sin A\cos B = \sin(A + B) + \sin(A - B)$, $2\cos A\sin B = \sin(A + B) - \sin(A - B)$, $2\cos A\cos B = \cos(A + B) + \cos(A - B)$, $2\sin A\sin B = \cos(A - B) - \cos(A + B)$.

In a proof pair the angles so that the half-sum is the same in the numerator and the denominator.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How ISC marks are usually awarded**
- *Exact value (2 marks):* the split of the angle, then the surd.
- *Given ratios (3 marks):* the missing ratios with signs, the formula, the answer.
- *Identity (3 marks):* expansion or pairing, simplification, conclusion.
- *Half-angle value (3 marks):* the quadrant of the half angle, the formula, the answer.
- *Section D (5 marks):* questions come in parts such as 2 + 3; label each part and give a mark's worth of working per step.

**Common mistakes**
- Writing $\sin(A + B) = \sin A + \sin B$.
- Using $+$ between the products in $\cos(A + B)$.
- Taking the sign of a half-angle ratio from the quadrant of $x$ instead of $\dfrac{x}{2}$.
- Forgetting the minus sign in $\cos C - \cos D$.
- Using $\tan(A + B)$ where $\tan A\tan B = 1$ or an angle is $90^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: The expansion of $\sin(P - Q)$ in terms of the sines and cosines of $P$ and $Q$ is
questions.solution_md: The sine formula keeps the sign of the angle: $\sin(P - Q) = \sin P\cos Q - \cos P\sin Q$. Option (b) is $\sin(P + Q)$ and (c) is $\cos(P + Q)$.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is a correct expansion of $\cos(P + Q)$ for all angles $P$ and $Q$?
questions.solution_md: The cosine of a sum reverses the sign between the two products: $\cos(P + Q) = \cos P\cos Q - \sin P\sin Q$. Option (a) is $\cos(P - Q)$.

questions.stem_md: The exact value of $\sin 195^\circ$ is
questions.solution_md: $195^\circ = 150^\circ + 45^\circ$, so $\sin 195^\circ = \sin 150^\circ\cos 45^\circ + \cos 150^\circ\sin 45^\circ = \dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} - \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2} - \sqrt{6}}{4}$. It is negative, as the third quadrant requires.

questions.stem_md: The value of $\tan 105^\circ$ is
questions.solution_md: $\tan 105^\circ = \tan(60^\circ + 45^\circ) = \dfrac{\sqrt{3} + 1}{1 - \sqrt{3}} = -\dfrac{(\sqrt{3} + 1)^2}{2} = -(2 + \sqrt{3})$. The angle is in the second quadrant, where tangent is negative.

questions.stem_md: The acute angles $A$ and $B$ satisfy $\sin A = \dfrac{7}{25}$ and $\cos B = \dfrac{3}{5}$. The value of $\sin(A + B)$ is
questions.solution_md: $\cos A = \dfrac{24}{25}$ and $\sin B = \dfrac{4}{5}$, so $\sin(A + B) = \dfrac{7}{25}\cdot\dfrac{3}{5} + \dfrac{24}{25}\cdot\dfrac{4}{5} = \dfrac{21 + 96}{125} = \dfrac{117}{125}$. The value $\dfrac{21}{125}$ is only the first product.

questions.stem_md: The acute angles $x$ and $y$ satisfy $\tan x = 3$ and $\tan y = 2$. Then $x + y$ equals
questions.solution_md: $\tan(x + y) = \dfrac{3 + 2}{1 - 6} = -1$. Each angle is acute, so $0 < x + y < \pi$, and the only angle there with tangent $-1$ is $\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$.

questions.stem_md: The value of $\sin 80^\circ\cos 20^\circ - \cos 80^\circ\sin 20^\circ$ is
questions.solution_md: The expression has the form $\sin P\cos Q - \cos P\sin Q = \sin(P - Q)$ with $P = 80^\circ$, $Q = 20^\circ$, so it equals $\sin 60^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.

questions.stem_md: The expression $\cos 40^\circ\cos 10^\circ - \sin 40^\circ\sin 10^\circ$ is equal to
questions.solution_md: The pattern $\cos P\cos Q - \sin P\sin Q$ is $\cos(P + Q)$, here $\cos 50^\circ$. Option (c) would need a plus sign between the products.

questions.stem_md: For every real $x$, the double angle $\sin 2x$ equals
questions.solution_md: Put $B = A = x$ in $\sin(A + B) = \sin A\cos B + \cos A\sin B$ to get $2\sin x\cos x$. Option (b) is always $1$.

questions.stem_md: Exactly one of the four expressions below is **not** equal to $\cos 2\theta$ for all $\theta$. Which one?
questions.solution_md: The three forms $1 - 2\sin^2\theta$, $2\cos^2\theta - 1$ and $\cos^2\theta - \sin^2\theta$ all equal $\cos 2\theta$. The expression $2\sin^2\theta - 1$ is $-\cos 2\theta$.

questions.stem_md: If $\sin\theta = \dfrac{15}{17}$ and $\theta$ is acute, the value of $\sin 2\theta$ is
questions.solution_md: $\cos\theta = \dfrac{8}{17}$, so $\sin 2\theta = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta = 2\cdot\dfrac{15}{17}\cdot\dfrac{8}{17} = \dfrac{240}{289}$. Option (b) forgets the factor $2$ and (d) is $\cos 2\theta$.

questions.stem_md: When $\tan x = \dfrac{3}{8}$, the value of $\tan 2x$ is
questions.solution_md: $\tan 2x = \dfrac{2\tan x}{1 - \tan^2 x} = \dfrac{3/4}{1 - 9/64} = \dfrac{3/4}{55/64} = \dfrac{48}{55}$. Option (b) uses $1 + \tan^2 x$, which is the formula for $\sin 2x$.

questions.stem_md: The acute angle $x$ satisfies $\cos 2x = \dfrac{7}{25}$. Then $\tan x$ equals
questions.solution_md: Since $\tan^2 x = \dfrac{1 - \cos 2x}{1 + \cos 2x} = \dfrac{18/25}{32/25} = \dfrac{9}{16}$ and $x$ is acute, $\tan x = \dfrac{3}{4}$. The value $\dfrac{9}{16}$ is $\tan^2 x$.

questions.stem_md: For every real $A$, the cosine of the triple angle, $\cos 3A$, is equal to
questions.solution_md: Writing $3A = 2A + A$ and using the double angle formulae gives $\cos 3A = 4\cos^3 A - 3\cos A$. Option (c) is the formula for $\sin 3A$ with $\sin$ replaced by $\cos$ and is wrong.

questions.stem_md: If $\sin x = \dfrac{3}{10}$, then $\sin 3x$ equals
questions.solution_md: $\sin 3x = 3\sin x - 4\sin^3 x = 0.9 - 4(0.027) = 0.9 - 0.108 = 0.792$. Option (d) stops after $3\sin x$ and (b) reverses the order of the two terms.

questions.stem_md: In terms of $\cos x$, the half-angle square $\sin^2\dfrac{x}{2}$ equals

questions.stem_md: The angles $A$, $B$, $C$ of a triangle satisfy $\tan A = 2$ and $\tan B = 3$. The value of $\tan C$ is
questions.solution_md: $C = 180^\circ - (A + B)$, so $\tan C = -\tan(A + B) = -\dfrac{2 + 3}{1 - 6} = 1$. As a check, $\tan A + \tan B + \tan C = 6 = \tan A\tan B\tan C$.

questions.stem_md: Using the formula for $\tan(A + B)$ twice, show that $\tan(A + B + C) = \dfrac{a + b + c - abc}{1 - ab - bc - ca}$, where $a = \tan A$, $b = \tan B$ and $c = \tan C$.

Multiply the numerator and the denominator by $1 - ab$: the numerator becomes $a + b + c(1 - ab) = a + b + c - abc$ and the denominator becomes $1 - ab - c(a + b) = 1 - ab - bc - ca$. Hence the result.

questions.stem_md: Prove that $\dfrac{\sin 5x - \sin 3x}{\cos 5x + \cos 3x} = \tan x$.

answer.model_answer_md: Half-sum $= 4x$ and half-difference $= x$. $\sin 5x - \sin 3x = 2\cos 4x\sin x$ and $\cos 5x + \cos 3x = 2\cos 4x\cos x$. Dividing, the common factor $2\cos 4x$ cancels and $\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x} = \tan x$.

questions.solution_md: The same half-sum appears in both products.

questions.stem_md: Show that $\dfrac{\cos 35^\circ + \cos 85^\circ}{\sin 85^\circ - \sin 35^\circ} = \cot 25^\circ$.

answer.model_answer_md: $\cos 35^\circ + \cos 85^\circ = 2\cos 60^\circ\cos 25^\circ$ and $\sin 85^\circ - \sin 35^\circ = 2\cos 60^\circ\sin 25^\circ$. The common factor $2\cos 60^\circ$ cancels, leaving $\dfrac{\cos 25^\circ}{\sin 25^\circ} = \cot 25^\circ$.

questions.solution_md: Half-sum of the angles is $60^\circ$ in both, half-difference is $25^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: Prove that $\cos 4x\cos x - \cos 6x\cos 3x = \sin 7x\sin 2x$.

answer.model_answer_md: $\cos 4x\cos x = \dfrac{1}{2}(\cos 5x + \cos 3x)$ and $\cos 6x\cos 3x = \dfrac{1}{2}(\cos 9x + \cos 3x)$. Subtracting, the $\cos 3x$ terms cancel: $\dfrac{1}{2}(\cos 5x - \cos 9x) = \dfrac{1}{2}\cdot 2\sin 7x\sin 2x = \sin 7x\sin 2x$.

questions.solution_md: Product to sum twice, then sum to product once.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Using $\cos(A - B) = \cos A\cos B + \sin A\sin B$, derive $\cos(A + B)$, and then derive $\sin(A + B)$. [3]

(b) Hence find the exact value of $\sin 255^\circ$. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Replace $B$ by $-B$: $\cos(A + B) = \cos A\cos(-B) + \sin A\sin(-B) = \cos A\cos B - \sin A\sin B$.

For the sine, $\sin(A + B) = \cos(90^\circ - (A + B)) = \cos((90^\circ - A) - B) = \cos(90^\circ - A)\cos B + \sin(90^\circ - A)\sin B = \sin A\cos B + \cos A\sin B$.

(b) $255^\circ = 210^\circ + 45^\circ$, so $\sin 255^\circ = \sin 210^\circ\cos 45^\circ + \cos 210^\circ\sin 45^\circ = -\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} - \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} = -\dfrac{\sqrt{2} + \sqrt{6}}{4}$.

questions.solution_md: Substitute $-B$; shift by $90^\circ$ for the sine; split $255^\circ$ in the third quadrant.

questions.stem_md:
The acute angles $A$, $B$ and $C$ satisfy $\tan A = \dfrac{1}{3}$, $\tan B = \dfrac{1}{5}$ and $\tan C = \dfrac{3}{11}$.

(a) Find $\tan(A + B)$. [2]

(b) Using your answer, find $\tan(A + B + C)$. [2]

(c) State, with a reason, the value of $A + B + C$ in degrees. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\tan(A + B) = \dfrac{\frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{5}}{1 - \frac{1}{3}\cdot\frac{1}{5}} = \dfrac{8/15}{14/15} = \dfrac{4}{7}$.

(b) $\tan(A + B + C) = \dfrac{\frac{4}{7} + \frac{3}{11}}{1 - \frac{4}{7}\cdot\frac{3}{11}} = \dfrac{65/77}{65/77} = 1$.

(c) Each tangent is less than $1$, so each angle is below $45^\circ$ if it is acute, and the sum lies between $0^\circ$ and $135^\circ$. The only angle in that range with tangent $1$ is $45^\circ$, so $A + B + C = 45^\circ$.

questions.solution_md: Add two angles first and then the third; bound the sum to name the angle.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Starting from $\sin(2x + x)$, prove that $\sin 3x = 3\sin x - 4\sin^3 x$. [3]

(b) Find $\sin 3x$ when $\sin x = \dfrac{7}{25}$. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\sin 3x = \sin 2x\cos x + \cos 2x\sin x = (2\sin x\cos x)\cos x + (1 - 2\sin^2 x)\sin x = 2\sin x\cos^2 x + \sin x - 2\sin^3 x$. Replacing $\cos^2 x$ by $1 - \sin^2 x$: $2\sin x - 2\sin^3 x + \sin x - 2\sin^3 x = 3\sin x - 4\sin^3 x$.

(b) $\sin 3x = 3\cdot\dfrac{7}{25} - 4\cdot\dfrac{343}{15625} = \dfrac{13125}{15625} - \dfrac{1372}{15625} = \dfrac{11753}{15625}$.

questions.solution_md: Expand with the sum formula; reduce to $\sin x$ only; then substitute.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Prove that $\tan\dfrac{x}{2} = \dfrac{1 - \cos x}{\sin x} = \dfrac{\sin x}{1 + \cos x}$. [3]

(b) Use the second form with $x = 30^\circ$ and the first form with $x = 45^\circ$ in suitable places to find the exact values of $\tan 15^\circ$ and $\tan 22.5^\circ$. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\tan\dfrac{x}{2} = \dfrac{\sin(x/2)}{\cos(x/2)}$. Multiply top and bottom by $2\sin\dfrac{x}{2}$: $\dfrac{2\sin^2(x/2)}{2\sin(x/2)\cos(x/2)} = \dfrac{1 - \cos x}{\sin x}$.

Multiply top and bottom instead by $2\cos\dfrac{x}{2}$: $\dfrac{2\sin(x/2)\cos(x/2)}{2\cos^2(x/2)} = \dfrac{\sin x}{1 + \cos x}$.

(b) With $x = 30^\circ$: $\tan 15^\circ = \dfrac{1 - \sqrt{3}/2}{1/2} = 2 - \sqrt{3}$. With $x = 45^\circ$: $\tan 22.5^\circ = \dfrac{\sin 45^\circ}{1 + \cos 45^\circ} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}/2}{1 + \sqrt{2}/2} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2 + \sqrt{2}} = \sqrt{2} - 1$.

questions.solution_md: Multiply by the sine for one form and by the cosine for the other; then substitute.

questions.stem_md:
(a) By putting $A = \dfrac{C + D}{2}$ and $B = \dfrac{C - D}{2}$ in $\cos(A + B) + \cos(A - B)$, deduce a product form of $\cos C + \cos D$. [3]

(b) Hence find the exact value of $\cos 105^\circ + \cos 15^\circ$. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\cos(A + B) + \cos(A - B) = (\cos A\cos B - \sin A\sin B) + (\cos A\cos B + \sin A\sin B) = 2\cos A\cos B$.

With $A + B = C$ and $A - B = D$, we have $A = \dfrac{C + D}{2}$ and $B = \dfrac{C - D}{2}$. So $\cos C + \cos D = 2\cos\dfrac{C + D}{2}\cos\dfrac{C - D}{2}$.

(b) Take $C = 105^\circ$, $D = 15^\circ$: $\cos 105^\circ + \cos 15^\circ = 2\cos 60^\circ\cos 45^\circ = 2\cdot\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$.

questions.solution_md: Add the two cosine formulae; then name $C$ and $D$.

questions.stem_md:
Prove that $\dfrac{\sin 5A - 2\sin 3A + \sin A}{\cos 5A - \cos A} = \tan A$.

(a) Combine $\sin 5A + \sin A$. [1]

(b) Simplify the numerator. [2]

(c) Write $\cos 5A - \cos A$ as a product. [1]

(d) Divide and complete the proof. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\sin 5A + \sin A = 2\sin 3A\cos 2A$.

(b) The numerator is $2\sin 3A\cos 2A - 2\sin 3A = 2\sin 3A(\cos 2A - 1) = -4\sin 3A\sin^2 A$, using $\cos 2A - 1 = -2\sin^2 A$.

(c) $\cos 5A - \cos A = -2\sin 3A\sin 2A$.

(d) $\dfrac{-4\sin 3A\sin^2 A}{-2\sin 3A\sin 2A} = \dfrac{2\sin^2 A}{2\sin A\cos A} = \dfrac{\sin A}{\cos A} = \tan A$.

questions.solution_md: Pair the outer terms of the numerator; keep $\sin 3A$ as the common factor.

questions.stem_md:
Let $P = \cos 20^\circ\cos 40^\circ\cos 80^\circ$.

(a) Use a product-to-sum formula to write $\cos 20^\circ\cos 40^\circ$ as a sum. [2]

(b) Multiply by $\cos 80^\circ$, use a product-to-sum formula again, and hence show that $P = \dfrac{1}{8}$. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\cos 20^\circ\cos 40^\circ = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\cos 60^\circ + \cos 20^\circ\right] = \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{2}\cos 20^\circ$.

(b) $P = \dfrac{1}{4}\cos 80^\circ + \dfrac{1}{2}\cos 20^\circ\cos 80^\circ$. Now $\cos 20^\circ\cos 80^\circ = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\cos 100^\circ + \cos 60^\circ\right] = \dfrac{1}{2}\cos 100^\circ + \dfrac{1}{4}$. So $P = \dfrac{1}{4}\cos 80^\circ + \dfrac{1}{4}\cos 100^\circ + \dfrac{1}{8}$. Because $\cos 100^\circ = -\cos 80^\circ$, the first two terms cancel and $P = \dfrac{1}{8}$.

questions.solution_md: Two rounds of product to sum; the terms in $\cos 80^\circ$ cancel.
